newsitem.title: USA: Stocks hit fifth record in 1997, dollar soars.
newsitem.headline: Stocks hit fifth record in 1997, dollar soars.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average eked out its fifth record of the year Monday, but bonds fell as investors braced for a round of new economic data.
The dollar rose to new two-year highs against most European currencies amid supportive comments from German and U.S. officials.

The 30-stock Dow index rose 5.39 points to 6,709.18, surpassing Friday's record finish of 6,703.79. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,366 to 1,159 on active volume of 443 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The market also was devoid of the volatility that has marked trading since the start of the year.
J.P. Morgan & Co. Inc. was the strongest performer among Dow components, rising $2.75 to $102.50 after reporting stronger-than-expected fourth quarter earnings.
The bank's results triggered a rally in financial shares, but analysts said activity appeared restrained ahead of Tuesday's release of the consumer price index for December.
Oil stocks, the big winners last week, fell broadly following a sharp drop in crude oil prices.
"When you start profit-taking you have to go where the profits are," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest. "Clearly the oil shares have been strong performers lately."

Elsewhere, the market was noticeably muted and stocks held to fairly tight ranges. The session was the first this year that failed to produce a move of 50 points in the Dow index to trigger the NYSE's programme trading curbs.
"Today was a moment to breathe," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "We still saw evidence that profit-taking is short-lived, shallow and greeted with buyers."
Stocks got little help from bonds as the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slipped 2/32 point, leaving its yield unchanged at Friday's close of 6.85 percent, which was up from 6.75 percent on Thursday.
Despite the recent rise in interest rates, some analysts saw reason for optimism.
"What stuck out more than anything were the utilities, where we saw some buying," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
The dollar rose to 1.5925 German marks, its highest level since August 1994, before fetching 1.5883 marks in late trading vs. Friday's 1.5859 marks.
The dollar climbed to 1.3796 Swiss francs, its highest level since May 1994, before ending at 1.3765 Swiss francs. The dollar closed lower at 1.3760 Swiss francs on Friday.
The dollar rose to 116.49 Japanese yen from 116.13 yen.
Oil prices sank after forecasts of warmer temperatures in the U.S. Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market, triggered a sell-off in heating oil.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange, February heating oil closed down a sharp 2.45 cents a gallon at 69.70 cents.
Pressured by heating oil's sharp drop, February crude closed down 90 cents a barrel at $25.19 and February gasoline down 2.27 cents a gallon at 68.09 cents.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices posted three-month highs with gains fed for a second straight day supported by worries about hot weather in South America and smaller U.S. stocks.
January soybeans peaked at $7.38 per bushel early Monday, topping the high of $7.37 set on October 11. The contract closed at $7.32-3/4, up 6 cents.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed at the day's best level, up 50.7 points at 4,107.3, and within reach of its Dec. 31 high of 4,118.5. In Tokyo, the Nikkei average of 225 leading issues, soared 815.14 points to finish at 18,118.79.
